articleTitle: The electrical breakdown of insulating oil
abstract: The author attempts to reconcile the various approaches to the mechanism of breakdown in insulating liquids. The author argues that a breakdown model is necessary if sensible use is to be made of the abundance of practical data which has been accumulated. Models are proposed based on the latest information and the effects of particles, water and dissolved gas discussed in the light of these models. The partial discharge initiated at an electrode is proposed as the key mechanism in the breakdown process. This initial discharge must exceed a critical value for a local discharge to become the precursor to a breakdown. Particulate contamination is clearly important in facilitating a local discharge. Electrical breakdown is a weaklink process. Only one unusually large discharge (for example from an exceptionally large particle) is necessary to cause a breakdown of the system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Power system reliability and its assessment. 2. Composite generation and transmission systems
abstract: For pt.1 see ibid., vol.6, no.4, p.191-6 (1992). The authors consider the integrated effect of generation and transmission systems, sometimes referred to the second hierarchical level (HL II). The purpose of assessing the reliability of the power system at this level is to estimate the ability of the system to perform its function of moving the energy provided by the generation system to the bulk supply points.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Power system reliability and its assessment. I. Background and generating capacity
abstract: The functional zones of a power system (generation, transmission and distribution) can be divided into three hierarchical levels. The first level relates to generation facilities which are considered in this article. The authors discuss generation capacity requirements, probabilistic criteria and indices, and reliability evaluation. The modelling approach, peak load effect and generation expansion planning are also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electromagnetic compatibility. I. General principles
abstract: Electromagnetic compatibility has become an important engineering discipline, essential for the proper design of all types of equipment incorporating electrical and electronic circuits. In this part of the tutorial the author discusses the general principles of EMC identifies the major sources of interference, the range and features of the coupling mechanisms, and some of the effects of interference on equipment. The ever-changing international scene regarding standards and EMC regulations are also described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Partial-discharge measurements for insulation quality
abstract: There is one common factor that, in different forms, runs throughout the entire electrical and electronics industries. That factor is the requirement for insulation that gives the necessary mechanical, thermal and electrical properties needed for particular applications. The presence of partial discharges indicates some defect within the insulation that is very likely to affect the expected life of the particular item. Partial-discharge testing techniques can therefore offer a very sensitive means of assessing insulation quality either on individual component parts or on complete equipment assemblies. The author describes the aims and applications of the technique and also tackles the practical problems that can be encountered. The author discusses the discharge mechanism and detection techniques. Routine and on-site testing are discussed. The effects of interference and interference rejection also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electromagnetic compatibility. II. Design principles
abstract: For pt.I see ibid., vol.6, no.2, p.89-94 (1992). All types of equipment and systems must be designed to meet electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) specifications. To achieve this aim, special design techniques are necessary. Their effective use in practical applications depends on the understanding of the underlying physical principles. EMC problems involve complex electromagnetic interactions and hence can only be tackled effectively by a combination of experimental and numerical tools. In this part of the tutorial the general principles and techniques underlying all EMC design are described. These include filtering, shielding, earthing, CAD in EMC, and EMC testing.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design considerations for static auxiliary supplies
abstract: The author discusses the way in which different design techniques are used to satisfy railway operators' requirements for static auxiliary supplies. Design options for voltage and frequency control are considered and design solutions for the Hong Kong Mass Transit Railway Corporation are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Overhead line design in relation to electric and magnetic field limits
abstract: Designers of overhead power lines have to contend with many technical and economic factors in their work. More recently, yet another has been added to the list-electric and magnetic fields. The author points out the principal design features which affect the fields from lines, and summarises the guidelines and standards which exist around the world for power-frequency fields.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electroheat and the ionised state
abstract: A number of electroheat processes operate through the formation of an ionised state primarily in the form of a glow or an arc discharge. The author looks at normal glow discharges; the energy source for the CO/sub 2/ laser, plasma chemistry and surface treatment; abnormal glow discharges: carburising and nitriding surface treatments; and arc discharges; the energy source for Nd:YAG and ruby lasers, plasma chemistry, plasma arc for cutting, welding or spraying, plasma furnaces, arc furnace for metal melting, and arc welding.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: 'Curtain' electron beam processor technology and applications. II. Applications
abstract: For pt.I see ibid., vol.6, no.3, p.111 (1992). The authors discuss the diverse applications of curtain electron beam processors capable of delivering beam currents of as much as 1000 mA at accelerating voltages of up to 300 kV. The main applications are: radiation curing (Radcure); crosslinking/vulcanisation; sterilisation; and power station flue-gas cleaning. In particular, the radiation curing application is very broad and includes the curing of many different coatings, inks, fillers, resins and adhesives for many different purposes. The advantages of electron beam technology over thermal and UV curing are discussed. The authors then describe use of electron beams in the applications mentioned.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electromagnetic compatibility for the power engineer
abstract: The new European Community directive on electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) will be issued on the 3rd May 1989. The author discusses implementation of the directive; the electromagnetic environment; designing for immunity; and testing for EMC.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Power system stability. 3. Improved modelling and new work
abstract: For pt.2 see ibid., vol.5, no.4, p.191 (1991). It is obvious that computer models of power systems are only as good as the data used. A generator model is often included in these computer models but a good model greatly increases computing time. The author looks at how to obtain the data necessary for computer modelling when designing new generators.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Fuel cells are coming to town
abstract: The author looks at the state of the art developments in fuel cell technology worldwide. Molten carbonate, solid oxide and phosphoric acid fuel cells are looked at in particular. The use of fuel cells in power plants is also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A new approach to maintenance-free industrial batteries
abstract: The ideal of a completely maintenance-free battery has existed in the battery industry for many years, but has only become a reality for industrial batteries within the last decade. The author looks at the design of maintenance-free nickel-cadmium batteries and charts their development. The active material is retained in perforated steel pockets so there is virtually no shedding of active material during the life of the battery.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electricity and the built environment of the future
abstract: Buildings account for nearly half of the UK total energy use and it is therefore imperative that the best energy technologies are adopted in both new and refurbished buildings. The author discusses energy efficiency in heating and air conditioning systems. Energy storage by use of ice storage, eutectic salts and by using the fabric of the buildings, is discussed. The author then discusses 'healthy' buildings including the need for fresh-air ventilation and heat recovery, displacement ventilation, and the control and monitoring of air quality.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Power to move people for the Manchester Metrolink
abstract: Modern light rail rapid transit is gaining in popularity and the right power supply equipment is important for the reliable operation of any railway service. The author reviews the design process and equipment supplied to achieve this goal for the Manchester Metrolink. The depth of work and design methods employed to arrive at adequate but cost-effective equipment ratings is presented along with an insight into some of the forward thinking, which has been employed to cater for future requirements. The author discusses the substations, AC and DC switchgear, rectifiers, transformers, overhead line equipment, stray current control, and touch voltages.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Parallel operation of generating plant within a public electricity supply network
abstract: The privatisation of the electricity supply distribution networks in late 1990 has established the legality for private persons or companies to use these networks as a means of transmitting energy from one location to another or to third parties. With this increasing number of private generators, the need to control the quality of supply and safeguard the general public are receiving increasing prominence. The author considers requirements, islanding and CHP schemes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The protection of the overhead system in Northern Electric
abstract: Northern Electric's overhead system consists of approximately 5500 km of 20 kV line and 5000 km of 11 kV line. Both systems are subjected to the same range of fault causes which afflicts most overhead systems. The author assesses protection performance and continuous monitoring and discusses systems which will result in optimum performance of the two networks. Systems looked at include a group-fused system; variable fuse size and triggered gap systems; automatic sectionalisers; and mixed solid fused systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Innovatory developments in infrared process heating
abstract: The author looks at the use of infrared for industrial process heating where power requirements can vary from a few hundred watts to several megawatts. For process heating IR radiation in the wavelength range of 0.8 to about 10 mu m is used. Control, efficiency, modelling and oven design are all discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electrical services in the International Convention Centre, Birmingham
abstract: The International Convention Centre, Birmingham (ICCB) is intended for: international and national conferences (with 12 language interpretation), concerts, exhibitions, product launches, banquets, meetings, and for being a social centre for the people of Birmingham. The author describes the design constraints on the ICCB and outlines the main facilities. The author then describes the electricity supply to the ICCB including the HV distribution, LV distribution, and protection of the system. The author also describes the lighting, emergency lighting and fire alarm system. Other services are briefly mentioned.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: 'Curtain' electron beam processor technology and applications. 1. The technology
abstract: Electron beam processors have advanced a long way since the early scanned beam systems associated with radiation research and radiography. 'Curtain' beam equipment is today used in a wide range of industrial processes such as printing, magnetic media manufacture and the crosslinking of plastic film and wire insulation. The authors describe the technology that has been developed to deliver beam currents of as much as 1000 mA at accelerating voltages of up to 300 kV.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Infrared adsorption measurements in the field using LED sources
abstract: Infrared absorption measurements allow the concentrations of specific liquids and gases to be measured. When infrared light-emitting-diode (LED) sources are employed, the infrared monitor can be made compact, low-powered and stable, and therefore suitable for portable applications. The characteristics and advantages of LED technology are discussed, and examples are given of commercial instruments developed to measure moisture in oil and carbon dioxide in air.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Real-time optimisation for power generation and CHP
abstract: Operators of power generation and combined heat and power plant need to make decisions on a regular basis. Some of these decisions relate to safety, engineering and contractual matters, where there is often no room for manoeuvre; the rest could be considered as degrees of freedom in the sense that there is choice in the way that the overall objectives are met. It would be misleading, however, to conclude that the latter choices are in any sense arbitrary, they often have an impact on the overall economics of the plant. The author explains how the above constitutes a modelling and optimisation problem which can be solved in a number of ways using currently available, proven hardware and software, gives examples of applications in CHP/power-generation plants, and indicates the scale of the potential benefits, in terms of reduction in energy usage.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A fire scenario-related evaluation of different types of transformers and the standards governing their classification and installation
abstract: The author sets out to show that the standards' impasse we are experiencing in the field of power and distribution transformers is due to the fact that standards committees are still asking the old askarel questions: 'Is it flammable or nonflammable?' Instead, in the context of the possibility of fire causation by a dielectric fluid, for both practical and criteriological reasons, the question should be whether the liquid is actually capable of maintaining a transient flame and thus capable of propagating a fire. If the author follows the argument that 'nonflammable' should be replaced by the much more relevant notion of 'nonpropagating'-and the test results shown make it difficult not to agree-then the author must set in motion the necessary procedures at IEC and CENELEC level.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Probabilistic methods applied to electric power systems-are they worth it?
abstract: The authors reflect on and question existing approaches to maintaining and improving the reliability of power systems and review and highlight some alternative ways forward. They also question the need and usefulness of present deterministic criteria and security standards and instead suggest that integrated cost benefit analyses involving customers and their decisions could be a more rewarding and applicable approach.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Lightning research: where do we go from here?
abstract: Thunderstorm activity in most of tropical Africa greatly exceeds that in industrialised countries, and lightning thus becomes a special problem for the tropical areas of the developing world of today. While research has produced many statistics, facts and theories concerning lightning phenomena, which are reviewed by the author, it also reveals many gaps and unknowns which must be taken account of in interpreting existing data. This leads finally to what in the author's opinion are the priorities for future lightning research especially in the context of Africa. Topics discussed by the author include thundercloud charge distribution, lightning strokes to earth, upward flashes, the attractive range of lightning, ground flash density, power line protection, buildings protection, and human and livestock protection.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Power policy and environmental issues in developing countries
abstract: Environmental degradation has emerged as a serious problem that further complicates the major energy issues that arose in the 1970s. The author examines electricity related environmental issues in the developing countries, that will increasingly shape the future role of the power engineering profession. The growth related power needs of the Third World and their financial implications, the potential for better energy management, the financial mechanisms and policies that can improve the performance of developing countries power utilities, and the treatment of environmental impacts are explored.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Competition, control and the common good (electricity supply industry)
abstract: The last 75 years have seen tremendous changes take place in the public supply of electricity in the UK. The author describes some of the major events which, some might argue, have delayed the introduction of a properly-developed electricity supply infrastructure. Much of the discussion relates to ownership and control in the early days-some of which is just as relevant today. The oft-cited saying that 'there is nothing new under the sun' is shown to apply to UK electricity supply just as it does to many other aspects of life. Observations on the politics involved and their influence on the engineering aspects of the industry are made also.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Failure analysis of HV motors in thermal station auxiliary systems
abstract: The authors analyse the failure data of HV motors from 35 power stations in India. The probable causes of the failures are discussed including insulation failure and switching overvoltages. The authors discuss insulation tests, a protection plan for the motors, and remedial measures and preventive maintenance. By scheduling testing and maintenance, the number of failures should be reduced and motor performance improved.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Harnessing the wind
abstract: In December 1991, Britain's first wind farm was connected to the grid. Concurrently in the latest NFFO round, proposals for 49 projects totalling almost 200 MW were approved by the Government. Wind power is on the verge of widespread commercial development in the UK. In this review the author looks at the technology of wind turbines, the economics and the environmental impact of wind farms.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Special problems in the installation of large electrical machines
abstract: Of the millions of rotating electrical machines sold each year, the majority are assembled in the ideal conditions of the maker's factory and shipped to the customer in one unit. At the large end of the range, however, a size is reached when transport and site handling limitations prevent this. It then becomes necessary either to modify the design of components or to assemble them on site. The authors describe the special problems that arose at site with two projects, Dinorwig, and JET where the option to build at site was chosen, and those that still arose with the QE2 refit when the ideal design of propulsion motor was modified to produce shippable elements.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Environmental factors affecting generation planning
abstract: The realisation of the fragility of the Earth's climate has suddenly impinged on the steady long-term planning of the electricity generation industry. Generation planners must cope with not only the environmental problems but also the efforts of politicians and economists to solve them.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
